data: Brief Encounters: The Short Story through Histories and Cultures

If brevity is indeed the soul of wit, then the short story is the fictional equivalent of modernity: it captures an instant, a hovering mood, a passing shadow. In fact, in some ways the short story is the arch-genre of modernity. In the early to mid-19th century, the modern metropolis was being forged by capital, migration and anonymity; here rapid industrialisation made demands on uninterrupted time; the telegraph and the railways atomised distance; photography made visualising of a moment possible. It is in that kind of a city where print modernity took sharp turns and the short story became one of the founding genres to mirror the harried, hurried, fleeting life in the new metropolis. It came to belong to a space in between a sketch and a tale, a fable and a saga, an anecdote and a long narrative. This course would look at the cultural and social origin of the short story; enquire into the ways in which it has transformed over the last century and a half; look at some of the critical approaches to it; and study its astonishing fecundity and flourish, including in the Indian subcontinent. In short, this course will be a survey of the genre as well as one which would look closely at some of its most representative specimens, and in several languages.
